fields.h1: Build a KYC Workflow With a Case File for Every Customer
fields.hero_description: Build a KYC workflow that opens a case for each new customer, sends every check to a named reviewer, and logs each decision.
fields.features_heading: Six Parts of a KYC Workflow Emergent Builds
fields.features_subheading: Each new customer gets one case that fills in as checks come back and reviewers decide.
fields.feature_1:
An intake form that opens a case

Emergent builds the intake form and the case database from your prompt. Each new customer's answers and uploads become one case, saved in a database you own and can query.
fields.feature_2:
ID documents read into fields

The app reads the name, birth date, and ID number from an uploaded license or passport. A field it is unsure of goes to a person, and each one is compared with what was typed.
fields.feature_3:
Your screening service, connected

Emergent connects the app to the verification or screening service you already use, through its API. Each result lands on the case, and a possible match keeps the account on hold.
fields.feature_4:
Risk ratings from rules you write

Write the factors your compliance team rates on, such as account type or expected monthly volume, and the app scores each case. A high rating goes to a senior reviewer.
fields.feature_5:
Alerts that carry a case number only

Reviewers get a Slack or email alert that names the case and links to it. Documents and birth dates stay in the database, and a case left overdue escalates to a manager you name.
fields.feature_6:
The KYC app's code, in your GitHub

Export the full code to your GitHub repository on paid plans. Anyone on your team can trace each screening and routing rule to the exact lines of code that run it in production.

plan.angle: The top results are vendor guides that list KYC stages (identification, due diligence, screening, monitoring) and sell verification software. This page shows the case-handling app around those checks: an intake form that opens a case, an ID document read into fields and compared with what the customer typed, beneficial owners collected for business accounts, possible watchlist matches held for a named reviewer, and periodic reviews scheduled by risk rating, with alerts that carry a case number and a link instead of documents. Regulatory facts are quoted from 31 CFR; the page never promises compliance, and the bank's compliance team sets every rule.
tab_stories: Quenmore Credit Union opens a checking account: the app reads the uploaded driver's license, the birth year on it differs from the one typed on the form, so case K-1182 goes to analyst Leontyne Bartholdy, whose Slack alert carries only the case number and a link.

Ridgemoor Community Bank opens a business account for Dunmarrow Coffee Roasters: the owners are listed at 50, 30 and 20 percent, so the app sends ID links to Gwendolen Strathearn and Prudencia Nwosu-Hart, the two at 25 percent or more, and not to Ottokar Granholm at 20 percent.

Saltreach Wealth Partners screens a new client in case K-2207: the connected screening service returns 1 possible match, the account stays on hold, and reviewer Benedikta Talmadge clears it because the listed person was born in 1958 and the client in 1987, with her note saved to the case.

Corvellan Payments reviews high-risk customers every 12 months, medium every 24 and low every 36: in March 46 reviews are due, 37 customers confirm their details through a link, and the 9 with no answer after 14 days go to analyst Cordelio Achebe-Lowe.
